info.name: AAuth
info.description: AAuth agent authorization (draft-hardt-oauth-aauth-protocol-11) as the aauth-go sandbox's demo resources perform it: the five resource access modes. The sandbox's resources publish an authorization endpoint rather than challenge on the API call, so the challenge variant is left out; the Petstore collection covers it.

item.name: Agent identity
item.description: The simplest mode: the resource only needs to know which agent is calling. The agent signs every request with its own key and presents its agent token, which binds that key to the agent's identifier. The resource checks the signature and decides on the agent's identity alone. It replaces API keys with cryptographic identity, with no person and no further tokens involved.

item.name: 1. Request agent token (web app)
item.description:
The agent generates a fresh ephemeral key and asks its agent provider for an agent token. It signs the request with the new key, and the Signature-Key header carries a naming JWT signed by its durable key, which vouches for the new key. The agent provider recognizes the durable key from enrollment, checks that the new key signed the request, and applies its policy.

This is the web app pattern from the AAuth Bootstrap guidance; the endpoint path is the agent provider's own. Enrollment came first: the user signed in and the agent registered its durable key. Other platforms differ: a mobile app keeps its durable key in the Secure Enclave or StrongBox and usually attests it with App Attest or Play Integrity at enrollment; a self-hosted agent publishes its own JWKS and issues its own agent token, with no request at all; workload identity is not yet covered by the guidance.

Source: draft-hardt-aauth-bootstrap-02 §8.1, §10.1; draft-hardt-httpbis-signature-key-09 §3.5

item.name: 3. HTTP Sig w/ agent_token
item.description:
The agent calls the resource. The request carries an HTTP message signature made with the agent's key, and the agent token travels in the Signature-Key header.

The agent signs every request with the key in the token's cnf; the verifier checks the signature against that key.

Source: draft-11 §5.3.2, §11.3.3

item.name: Resource-managed access (two-party)
item.description:
The resource runs its own authorization: its own login, consent screen or existing OAuth flow. It answers the agent's first request with a 202 asking for user interaction, the person completes the resource's own flow, and the resource hands the agent a session token. The agent sends that token back on later calls, always under its own signature, so the token is useless to anyone else.

Steps between other roles, not sent by this collection:

- 5. Person → Resource: Completes the resource's own login and consent

item.name: 3. HTTP Sig w/ agent_token
item.description:
The agent calls the resource, signed with its key and presenting its agent token.

Source: draft-11 §6.2

item.name: 6. GET pending URL
item.description:
The agent polls the pending URL, still signing every request with its key.

Source: draft-11 §11.8.3

item.name: 8. HTTP Sig w/ agent_token + Authorization: AAuth
item.description:
On later calls the agent returns the session token in Authorization: AAuth and includes that header in its signature, so a stolen session token alone is worthless.

The signature must cover the authorization header, so the session token cannot be replayed as a bearer token.

Source: draft-11 §6.3

item.name: Person identity
item.description: Federated login for agents. The agent asks its person server for a person token addressed to this resource and presents it instead of its agent token. The resource learns which person the agent acts for, as a directed identifier unique to this resource, and applies its own access control. The person server issues the token but is not in the path of any call.

item.name: 3. POST person_token_endpoint (HTTP Sig w/ agent_token)
item.description:
The agent asks its person server for a person token for the resource it wants to call. The request is signed with the agent's key and presents the agent token, and the signature covers the body through Content-Digest.

A body sent to a PS must be covered by the signature through Content-Digest and Content-Type (§11.3.3.1). The draft's own example in §7.1 omits them.

Source: draft-11 §7.1, §11.3.3.1

item.name: 5. HTTP Sig w/ person_token
item.description:
The agent calls the resource presenting the person token in place of its agent token. The token's cnf is the same key that signs the request.

The person token replaces the agent token in Signature-Key. Its cnf is the same key that signs, so verification works as before.

Source: draft-11 §7.1.3

item.name: PS authorization (three-party)
item.description:
Three-party authorization. The resource has no access server of its own, so it trusts the person server that vouched for the person. The agent asks the resource for access and receives a resource token addressed to its PS. The PS obtains the person's consent and issues an auth token that the resource enforces against the person's identifier and the granted scope.

Steps between other roles, not sent by this collection:

- 9. Agent → Person: Open interaction URL with code
- 10. Person → Person Server: Review and approve

item.name: 3. POST person_token_endpoint (HTTP Sig w/ agent_token)

Source: draft-11 §7.1, §11.3.3.1

item.name: 5. POST authorization_endpoint (HTTP Sig w/ person_token)
item.description:
The agent asks the resource's authorization endpoint for the scope it needs, presenting the person token so the resource knows who the access is for.

The signature does not cover this body: Content-Digest is required only toward PS and AS endpoints, unless the resource asks for it through additional_signature_components.

Source: draft-11 §6.6

item.name: 7. POST auth_token_endpoint w/ resource_token + presented_token
item.description:
The agent brings the resource token to its PS, along with the person token it presented to the resource and a short justification. The PS checks that agent_jkt matches the key that signed this request and that the presented token matches the resource token.

The PS checks agent_jkt against the key that signed this request (the agent's), and checks presented_token against the resource token's presented_jti, ps and sub.

Source: draft-11 §7.2.1, §11.3.3.1

item.name: 11. GET pending URL (Prefer: wait)
item.description:
Meanwhile the agent polls the pending URL with a signed GET, asking the PS to wait up to 45 seconds for an answer. Once the person approves, the response to this poll carries the result.

Polling switches to GET on the Location URL and does not resend the original body. Prefer: wait asks the PS to hold the response until it can answer.

Source: draft-11 §11.8.3

item.name: 13. GET /api/documents (HTTP Sig w/ auth_token)
item.description:
The agent calls the API presenting the auth token, signed with the same key.

The resource checks iss, aud, cnf against the signing key, sub and scope.

Source: draft-11 §9.4.2

item.name: Federated authorization (four-party)
item.description:
Four-party authorization. The resource has its own access server that evaluates resource policy. The resource token names that access server, so the person server, after obtaining consent, federates with it, presenting the resource token, the agent token and the person token. The access server issues the auth token, which travels back through the PS to the agent.

Steps between other roles, not sent by this collection:

- 9. Agent → Person: Open interaction URL with code
- 10. Person → Person Server: Review and approve
- 12. Person Server → Access Server: POST auth_token_endpoint w/ resource_token (HTTP Sig w/ jwks_uri)
